comment: Line budgets per file type, enforced by tests/checks/size.test.js. soft = a warning that a split is due; hard = a failure, split before extending. Line count is only a PROXY for what actually degrades a reader, which is one concept stated in two places saying slightly different things - and that is enforced directly by the one-home gate. Where the two disagree, the one-home gate wins: a longer single file beats the same rule restated in three shorter ones.
why-these-numbers: Source files sit at 400/600 so one read-file action captures a whole module cheaply. The previous 300/500 produced 41 per-file exceptions across 39 files - a registry of exemptions rather than a constraint, each carrying an exit plan nobody took. Raising the cap to what the repo had actually settled at, and requiring an acknowledgement rather than a bespoke cap, took that to one exception and fifteen acknowledgements.

exempt-trees.docs/sessions-archive/: Closed, read-only history. Never reflowed to a budget.
exempt-trees.supabase/migrations/: Applied migrations are immutable once run (CLAUDE.md). Their length tracks the schema they create, and editing one to fit a budget would rewrite history the database has already applied.

docs/STATE.md.note: TIGHTER than its extension, not looser. A fixed-size current state, overwritten each checkpoint and never grown. The 40-line cap is the point of the file.

docs/CHANGELOG.md.note: RAISED 2026-09-17 from the 600 default, as a HOLDING MEASURE and not a fix. The file had reached exactly 600 and could not take the one line the definition of done requires, so no user-facing change could be recorded at all. Its own seam is right: this file shrinks by RELEASE, not by split - Unreleased rolls into a dated heading and the file resets - and only the owner can cut one. Put it back to 600 at that point. Until then the ceiling buys room for roughly a dozen entries, which is a backlog of unreleased work, not a healthy file.

assets/css/components.css.seam: Re-judged 2026-09-07 at 586 lines, the revisit its previous note set at 550. Still not worth splitting, and the seam is now a real one rather than a hypothetical: the indexed content shell (.ref-layout, .ref-sidebar, .ref-toolbar and their 48rem breakpoint) is used by exactly two pages, the reference viewer and the platform page, so it could move to its own sheet. That trade is 1.5KB off 22 pages against one extra request on 2 - and this repo has already decided that direction once, removing 21 requests by merging two nav tools. It stays. Next trigger is the 600-line hard cap, where the shell is what leaves.

assets/css/roadmap-detail.css.seam: Not yet, at 533. It is the one stylesheet for the roadmap drawer and the executive board, loaded by modules/roadmap/ and - for the drawer - modules/sprints/. It grew on 23 Sep 2026 by the drawer's "Where it stands" brief and the .rm-em emphasis rule, both drawer concerns. The seam when it passes 550 is the executive board rules (.rmd-exec*, the department-first rollup) leaving for roadmap-exec.css: the sprint page loads this sheet for the drawer alone and pays for board rules it never uses, so that split now saves bytes on a page as well as lines.

assets/css/roadmap-views.css.seam: Not yet, and the closest of the stylesheets to a real seam: the board layouts share one coordinate model, so splitting means duplicating that model or inventing a shared file that is most of it. The seventh view - the sprint roadmap - tested that and did not split it: assets/css/sprints.css reuses .rmv-tl and carries only what is new to sprints. It then took in the board chrome (.rm-toolbar, .rm-icon-toggle, .rm-state) that both board pages need, which is why it grew - a shared sheet is the right home for a shared strip. Revisit at 550, where the seam is that chrome leaving for a sheet of its own once a third page wants it.

assets/css/tokens.css.seam: Do not split. Tokens plus the dark-theme overrides: inherently long, no logic, and every value in the design system resolves here. A tokens-dark.css would add a request to all 24 pages for no reading gain.

assets/js/pages/roadmap/detail.js.seam: Not yet, at 563 - one line over the 562 it stood at. The value helpers already left for detail-values.js, and on 23 Sep 2026 the current-state brief was built as its own file (detail-brief.js) rather than here, with the sprint-slot row collapsing onto the shared sprintWhen helper to pay for the wiring. The details and notes parsers are the next seam and the next addition to this file must take it.

assets/js/pages/roadmap/roadmap.js.seam: Not yet. The roadmap page already loads twelve modules and is the heaviest page in the site; a roadmap-fetch.js would make it thirteen. The page-load fetch and the phase/link enrichment in onAuthed are the seam when it passes 550.

assets/js/pages/roadmap/views.js.seam: Not yet. The four layout families are already separate files; what is left is the shared placement model they all read. Splitting it further means another request on the heaviest page. The context and placement helpers are the seam at 550.

docs/CHANGELOG.md.seam: Do not split: it would put 'what changed' in two places. It shrinks by RELEASE, not by split - Unreleased becomes a dated heading and the file resets. Read newest-first, so length costs a reader nothing.

docs/ROADMAP-INTAKE.md.seam: Never split. It is the ONE home for the confidence bands, and one-home.test.js fails if they are restated elsewhere. The last attempt to split this file is what put them in three places.

docs/plan/20-API-REFERENCE.md.seam: Closed workstream record. Folds into a short outcome at the next release, keeping the corrections table.

docs/plan/80-LOAD-SPEED.md.seam: Closed workstream record. Most of the length is the account of where the plan was wrong, which is the part a later wave needs. Folds into a short outcome at the next release, not before.

supabase/policies.sql.seam: Never split. This is the security boundary and 'which tables can be written, and by whom' must stay a single-pass question. It grows with every new table, so it is the one file here likely to reach the cap - when it does, raise the cap and say why, do not fragment the answer.

supabase/schema/30_work.sql.seam: The work-items domain in one file, most of its length being the rationale beside each constraint. work_documents and work_notes are the seam - they are intake concerns, not roadmap ones - when it passes 550.

supabase/seed.sql.seam: Do not split while it is one readable pass of sample rows. Length tracks the number of rows, not complexity. If it nears the hard cap, split per domain into a seed/ directory.

tests/checks/render-coverage.test.js.seam: A registry plus four gates over it. The seam is the COVERAGE map leaving for its own data file, the way tests/size-budget.json holds the numbers this file's gates would otherwise restate. Not yet: every entry carries the REASON it renders the way it does, and those reasons are read beside the assertion that enforces them - splitting them apart is how a reason stops being maintained. Revisit at 550, or the first time a second gate needs the same map.

tests/unit/roadmap/detail.test.js.seam: Splits by what it proves, not by size: the drawer-shape cases (sections, ordering, deliverable lists) from the value-rendering cases (benefit, facts, links). Not worth doing at 425 lines because both halves share one sample() fixture and one load(), so a split duplicates the fixture to save nothing a reader notices. Revisit at 550, when the fixture is worth extracting to tests/lib and the two halves can each import it.

tests/unit/roadmap/views.test.js.seam: Not worth splitting: the placement-ordering cases share one fixture with the rest, so a split duplicates the fixture. No runtime cost either way, so the only gain would be cosmetic. Revisit if the fixture itself is extracted.

assets/js/pages/roadmap/views-sprint.js.seam: Not yet, at 544, but this is the closest any file here sits to its revisit trigger. It took the split the previous acknowledgement pointed at - the workstream cards left for views-sprint-cards.js - and has since gained the second reading of the axis (columns as a priority scale) and the stream ordering that keeps the two tabs numbering the plan identically. Both are the same concern the file already owns: what the axis IS, and what order the streams sit in. The next seam, at 550 and now six lines away, is hide mode - it is view state rather than rendering, it draws nothing, and it would move with its markup in one piece. The next addition to this file should take that split rather than push past the trigger.

assets/css/layout.css.seam: Not yet, at 408. It carries two things: the nav (bar, search, results) and the page scaffold (measure, head, card grid). That IS a seam - they share no selector - but the nav is on all 24 pages and the scaffold is too, so splitting buys a second request everywhere and no reading gain. Revisit at 500, where the seam is the nav leaving for a nav.css.

assets/css/sprints.css.seam: Not yet, at 490. It took the split this entry previously named - the discussion cards left for assets/css/sprint-cards.css - and has since gained the priority-scale column heads, which are board chrome and belong with the axis they relabel. What is left is the board and only the board. The next seam, still at 550, is hide mode: it styles a view state rather than the board, it is the one block here that draws nothing, and it would move with its markup in one piece.

tests/unit/roadmap/views-sprint.test.js.seam: Not yet, at 425. It proves one surface - the sprint BOARD - from four angles: the axis and its two readings, the bars and their spans, external marking, and hide mode. Hide mode is the real seam, exactly as it is in the module this file tests (see the entry for assets/js/pages/roadmap/views-sprint.js): those six cases share no state with the rest beyond sample() and would move as one block. Splitting now would duplicate the fixture to save twenty-five lines, which is the trade every sibling acknowledgement here has already refused. Revisit at 550, or the first time the axis grows a third reading - two is what the toggle affords and a third would make the axis cases a file of their own.

why-acknowledgements-are-decisions: An acknowledgement is a DECISION not to split, with the condition that would change it - not a queued task. Every one below was re-judged on 2026-08-30 against a question the earlier exit plans did not ask: what does the split COST? Splitting a stylesheet or a page module adds an HTTP request to every page that loads it, and this repo has no build step to hide that. The same session had just removed 21 requests by merging two nav tools; reintroducing them to shorten a file that sits 120 lines under its hard cap would be a bad trade made for tidiness. So the answer for all fifteen is currently 'not yet', each with the trigger that would change it. Reaching the hard cap is always such a trigger.
